c.tagline: UNESCO medina, Roman mosaics, and Boujaffar's endless sand.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow city taxis are cheap and metered — ask for the meter (compteur). For trips between towns, shared louages (white minibuses with a coloured stripe) leave from the louage station when full and are the standard local way to reach Monastir, Kairouan, or Tunis.

emergency.note: 197 reaches the police (Sûreté), 190 the national ambulance (SAMU), and 198 civil protection and fire.

avoid.reason: Beach resort — site of a 2015 attack; remain vigilant at tourist sites

hood_desc: The walled 9th-century old town — a UNESCO World Heritage site — wrapped around the Ribat fortress, the Great Mosque, the kasbah with its mosaic-filled archaeological museum, and a warren of souks; best for first-timers who want the city's history and character on their doorstep.

The downtown grid just outside the medina walls around Avenue Habib Bourguiba and Place Farhat Hached, with the train station, banks, cafes, and everyday shops; a convenient, well-connected central base close to both the old town and the seafront.

The long Boujaffar beachfront and its palm-lined corniche promenade, packed with sunbathers by day and strolling families and cafes by night; a relaxed seaside base right on the sand in the middle of the city.

A residential and resort strip north of the centre along the coast toward Kantaoui, lined with mid-range and family beach hotels and quieter than downtown; suits travelers who want the beach with a calmer pace.

A purpose-built marina resort about 10 km north of Sousse, ringed with whitewashed Andalusian-style villas, yacht berths, golf, restaurants, and bars; the liveliest spot for dining and going out after dark.

water.note: Tap water is chlorinated but most visitors and many locals drink bottled.

transit.hours: Sahel Metro trains run roughly 5:00 AM to 10:00 PM; SORETRAS city buses run from early morning until about 9:00 PM.
transit.note: Sousse is the northern terminus of the Sahel Metro (Métro du Sahel), an above-ground light-rail line linking Sousse with Monastir and Mahdia down the coast. In-town SORETRAS city buses cover the rest, and yellow taxis and shared louages fill the gaps.
transit.pay: Sahel Metro and bus tickets are bought in cash at station windows or on board; there is no rechargeable smart card and fares are only a dinar or two.

bus: SNTRI intercity coaches to Tunis and other cities
Louages (shared taxis) to Monastir, Kairouan, and Tunis
train: SNCFT mainline trains to Tunis and Sfax

transit.m: Airport shuttle or transfer to Sousse (~40-50 min)
Taxi to Sousse city center (40-50 min)

tip.r: Service isn't included; rounding up or leaving about 5-10% at restaurants and cafes for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Couscous au poisson
food.desc: Coastal Tunisian couscous steamed over a harissa-spiked broth and topped with whole grouper or sea bream plus vegetables. Sunday food, done all week here.

places.name: Restaurant du Peuple
places.note: Family-run, generous set menus with soup, salad, brik and couscous at honest prices.

places.name: La Table du Chef
places.note: Repeatedly named for its couscous; small, popular, worth booking at lunch.

places.name: Le Mazarine
places.note: Marina-side kitchen doing Tunisian classics with more polish than the medina eateries.

food.name: Brik a l'oeuf
food.desc: A triangle of paper-thin malsouka pastry folded around tuna, parsley, capers and a whole egg, deep-fried so the yolk is still running.

places.name: El Ksar
places.note: Singled out in local guides for its brik; crisp shell, properly runny yolk.

places.name: Restaurant du Peuple
places.note: Brik arrives as part of the classic fixed menu; eat it with your hands, fast.

places.name: Marche Central de Sousse
places.note: Market food stalls fry brik to order for a fraction of restaurant prices.

food.name: Lablabi
food.desc: Chickpea soup poured over torn stale bread with olive oil, harissa, cumin, capers and often a poached egg. The Tunisian working breakfast.

places.name: Marche Central de Sousse
places.note: Best eaten mid-morning at the market counters where turnover is fastest.

places.name: Medina souk eateries
places.note: Small hole-in-the-wall places near the Ribat serving lablabi for a couple of dinars.

places.name: Restaurant du Peuple
places.note: Sit-down version if you would rather have a table and a menu in French.

food.name: Ojja merguez
food.desc: Eggs poached in a fiery tomato, pepper and harissa sauce with spicy merguez sausage, eaten straight from the pan with bread.

places.name: Restaurant du Peuple
places.note: Ajja and ojja are menu regulars; ask for it less spicy if you are unsure.

places.name: Restaurant Cafe Seles
places.note: Tunisian and Mediterranean cooking in a calm blue-and-white dining room.

places.name: Le Mazarine
places.note: Reliable marina option for ojja and other Tunisian standards.

food.name: Grilled sea bream
food.desc: Whole daurade or loup grilled over coals, dressed with olive oil and lemon and served with slata mechouia, the smoky roast pepper and tomato salad.

places.name: Port El Kantaoui marina
places.note: Row of harbour-view restaurants; pick your fish by weight from the ice display.

places.name: Restaurant Cafe Seles
places.note: Fresh catch grilled simply, popular with locals as well as visitors.

places.name: Restaurant du Peuple
places.note: Grilled fish and meats at medina prices, with big portions.

food.name: Makroudh
food.desc: Diamond-cut semolina pastries filled with spiced date paste, fried and drenched in honey syrup. Sold by weight and best eaten the day they are made.

places.name: Medina patisseries
places.note: Sweet shops along the main souk sell makroudh, kaak warka and baklava by weight.

places.name: Marche Central de Sousse
places.note: Market sweet stalls with high turnover, so the pastries stay fresh.

places.name: Dar Lella Khadija
places.note: Traditional courtyard house serving pastries with mint tea in painted-tile surroundings.

food.name: Mint tea with pine nuts
food.desc: Strong sweet green tea poured over fresh mint and a spoon of toasted pine nuts or almonds. Ordering one buys you an hour at the table.

places.name: Cafe Maure
places.note: Terrace views over the medina rooftops; the classic place to slow down.

places.name: Dar Lella Khadija
places.note: Tea served in traditional ware around a tiled courtyard; very calm.

places.name: Le Petit Cafe Maure
places.note: Small, atmospheric cafe in the heart of the old town, popular with locals.

food.name: Celtia beer
food.desc: Tunisia's own pale lager, brewed since 1951. Alcohol is limited to licensed venues, so look for it at marina bars and hotel terraces rather than the medina.

places.name: Port El Kantaoui marina terraces
places.note: Licensed waterfront bars where a cold Celtia is entirely unremarkable.

places.name: Boujaffar seafront hotel bars
places.note: Hotel terraces along the beach strip are the other reliable licensed option.

landmarks: Medina of Sousse
A UNESCO World Heritage walled old town of whitewashed lanes, ramparts and souks, among the finest examples of early Islamic coastal architecture.
Ribat of Sousse
An 8th-century fortified monastery whose watchtower rewards climbers with the definitive panorama over the medina's rooftops and harbour.
Great Mosque of Sousse
A fortress-like 9th-century Aghlabid mosque with crenellated walls and a serene arcaded courtyard, strikingly austere and beautiful.
Sousse Archaeological Museum
Housed in the medina's kasbah, it holds Tunisia's finest Roman mosaic collection after the Bardo, including the celebrated Triumph of Bacchus.
Kasbah and Khalef Tower
The medina's highest point, an ancient citadel whose 9th-century signal tower still serves as a lighthouse over the city.
Catacombs of the Good Shepherd
Kilometres of early-Christian underground burial galleries from the 2nd to 4th centuries, with thousands of tombs cut into soft rock.
Dar Essid Museum
An opulent 928-year-old aristocratic house in the medina, furnished as its Ottoman-era owners left it, with a tower café view.
Boujaffar Beach
Sousse's palm-lined city beach and corniche, a golden strand where locals promenade beside the Mediterranean at sunset.
Port El Kantaoui
A purpose-built Andalusian-style marina village north of Sousse, ringed by whitewashed arcades, golf courses and bobbing yachts.
Zaouia Zakkak
An Ottoman-era religious complex in the medina, instantly recognisable by Sousse's only octagonal, Turkish-style tiled minaret.

train.note: The Sahel Metro light rail links Sousse with Monastir and Mahdia along the coast, while SNCFT mainline trains run north to Tunis (~2 hrs) and south to Sfax.

bus.note: SNTRI intercity coaches and shared louages connect Sousse to Tunis, Kairouan, Sfax and beyond from the town's bus and louage stations.

ferry.note: Sousse's port handles cargo and fishing boats, and Port El Kantaoui just north is a leisure marina, but no scheduled passenger ferry calls at either. What sails from El Kantaoui are summer-season sightseeing and pirate-boat cruises, not transport. For a genuine crossing you need La Goulette in Tunis, about 140 km north, where CTN runs the car ferries to Marseille and Genoa (https://www.ctn.com.tn/), or Sfax for the Kerkennah Islands ferry.

full.blurb: Islam's fourth-holiest city and a UNESCO site, with the vast Great Mosque, the Aghlabid basins, and carpet souks about 60 km inland.
full.name: Kairouan

full.blurb: Home to one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheatres in the world, a colossal UNESCO-listed colosseum in the countryside.
full.name: El Jem

full.blurb: Former Fatimid capital on a slim peninsula, with a quiet medina, a fishing port, and some of the Sahel's best beaches.
full.name: Mahdia

half.blurb: Coastal town 20 km south with its film-famous Ribat, the Bourguiba Mausoleum, and a marina — an easy hop on the Sahel Metro.
half.name: Monastir

half.blurb: Whitewashed clifftop fishing village overlooking the sea about 30 km north, known for its esparto-grass crafts.
half.name: Hergla
